power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

text.text: Increased fasting insulin reflects insulin resistance and is as a precursor to type 2 diabetes and a risk factor for kidney, heart and liver diseases and mortality.

Cluster-specific fasting insulin polygenic scores (PS) characterize insulin resistance mechanisms based on insulin-related genetic associations with metabolic traits, and they have not been evaluated for liver outcomes.

We calculated seven previously developed FI cluster-specific PS, including non-diabetogenic (Preserved Insulin Secretion, Elevated Insulin Secretion, Proinsulin) and diabetogenic clusters (Adiposity-driven Hyperinsulinemia, Visceral Adiposity, Lipodystrophy, Liver/Lipid) in 12,631 participants of the Hispanic Community Healthy Study/Study of Latinos (HCHS/SOL), and tested their association with type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular, kidney and liver outcomes.
We also tested the association of FI clusters with indices of insulin homeostasis in additional 1,316 Hispanic individuals.
Among HCHS/SOL participants (mean age 46 years, 59% women, 20% with diabetes), we validated associations of FI cluster-specific PS and the 19 traits used to generate clusters.
The Lipodystrophy cluster was associated with type 2 diabetes (p-value =3.5 x 10 -5 ).

In addition, the Adiposity-driven Hyperinsulinemia cluster was associated with the hepatic steatosis index (p-value = 2.2 ×10 -17 ) and the fatty liver index (p-value = 1.7 ×10 -14 ), while the Liver/Lipid cluster with liver fibrosis (p-value = 1.5 ×10 -4 ) and lower kidney function (p-value = 5.2 x 10 -5 ).
The non-diabetogenic Elevated Insulin Secretion cluster-specific PS was associated with the disposition index (p = 0.0015).
These results support insulin resistance mechanisms implicated in type 2 diabetes, liver and kidney outcomes.
Diabetes impacts 12% of the United States population, with about 90-95% of cases being type 2 diabetes 1, 2 .
In 2024, the age-adjusted prevalence of diagnosed type 2 diabetes in Hispanics/Latinos was 11.8% compared to 7.1% in non-Hispanic white individuals 1 .
Type 2 diabetes is diagnosed at a rate 13% higher in Hispanics/Latinos than the total U.S. adult population 3 .

Incident CKD at visit 2 was defined by an eGFR <60 ml/min/1.73 m 2 and an eGFR decline ≥1 ml/min per year, or UACR ≥30 mg/g at visit 2 among participants with an eGFR≥ 60 ml/min/1.73 m 2 and a UACR <30 mg/g at baseline.

Genotyping.
Participants were genotyped using the Illumina HumanOmni2.5-8v1-1 array as previously described 19 .

Principal components (PCs) were calculated using PC-AiR 20 .
text.formatted: Principal components (PCs) were calculated using PC-AiR <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">20</ref> .

text.text: The PCs showed genetic differentiation within and among six self-identified background groups (Cuban, Dominican, Puerto Rican, Mexican, and Central and South American).
We removed 56 individuals with missing genetic background group.
Imputation was performed using the TOPMed freeze 8 reference panel from the TOPMed imputation server 21 , with Eagle v2.4 for phasing and Minimac4 for imputation 22, 23 .

To exclude type 1 diabetes among HCHS/SOL participants, we calculated the type 1 diabetes genetic risk score 2 (GRS2) developed by Sharp et al., which includes 67 single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) 11 .

text.text: The GRS2 distinguishes type 1 diabetes from type 2 diabetes based on a bimodal distribution, using an approximate cutoff point of 13.5 that includes 87.8% of patients with type 2 diabetes and excludes 82.7% of type 1 diabetes patients 11 .

text.text: Calculation of the FI clusters.
We used the published weights for 110 SNPs to calculate seven FI cluster-specific PS 15 .
text.formatted: We used the published weights for 110 SNPs to calculate seven FI cluster-specific PS <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">15</ref> .

text.text: Some SNPs contributed to multiple clusters.
The alleles in these clusterspecific PS were aligned for increasing insulin effects.
PS clusters were defined as Preserved IS, Elevated IS, Proinsulin, Adiposity-driven Hyperinsulinemia, Visceral Adiposity, Lipodystrophy and Liver/Lipid.

For each FI cluster, the number of effect alleles for increasing FI at variants were multiplied by their respective multi-ancestry weights and summed across cluster variants to calculate each cluster-specific PS.

We first tested each of the cluster-specific PS for associations with 19 traits used to cluster the FI SNPs: (a) among people without diabetes: fasting glucose, 2-hour glucose, HbA1c, HOMA-B and (b) overall sample: height, waist and hip circumference, waist/hip ratio, body mass index (BMI), HDL cholesterol, LDL cholesterol, triglycerides, body fat %, liver enzymes (AST, ALT), heart rate, PR interval, CRP, and urine albumin.
We used linear mixed-effects models adjusted for age, sex, genetic group, center and five PCs, and random effects for census tract, household, and genetic relatedness to account for study design.
Analyses for waist circumference, hip circumference, and waist/hip ratio were adjusted for BMI, while AST and ALT were natural log transformed.
Associations with a p-value <3.8 x 10 -4 were considered significant based on 133 tests (19 traits by seven FI clusters).
text.formatted: Associations with a p-value <3.8 x 10 -4 were considered significant based on 133 tests (19 traits by seven FI clusters).

text.text: We then tested the association of each cluster with prediabetes, type 2 diabetes and insulin treatment use.
The analysis for insulin use was only tested among individuals with type 2 diabetes, and individuals with diabetes were excluded from the prediabetes analyses.

We also tested additional liver measures that were not used in the original clustering):Fibrosis-4 (FIB-4) index for liver fibrosis 25 , hepatic steatosis index (HSI) 26 , fatty liver index (FLI) 25 and nonalcoholic fatty liver disease liver fibrosis score (NAFLD-LFS) 27 .
text.formatted: We also tested additional liver measures that were not used in the original clustering):Fibrosis-4 (FIB-4) index for liver fibrosis <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">25</ref> , hepatic steatosis index (HSI) <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">26</ref> , fatty liver index (FLI) <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">25</ref> and nonalcoholic fatty liver disease liver fibrosis score (NAFLD-LFS) <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">27</ref> .

text.text: FIB-4 and NAFLD-LFS were natural log transformed.
We used the same linear mixed-effects models described above for clustering traits.
We then tested associations of each PS cluster with ten outcomes: CKD, CAD, stroke, myocardial infarction, hypertension, prediabetes, type 2 diabetes, insulin use, eGFR, and albuminuria.
For the eGFR analysis, we used a linear mixed-effects model.
For all categorical outcomes, we used logistic mixed-effects models.
Models for CKD, eGFR, albuminuria, CAD, stroke, myocardial infarction, and hypertension were run separately by type 2 diabetes status, as well as jointly adjusting for type 2 diabetes status.

The Bonferroni-adjusted significance level for all secondary outcomes was considered to be 5.1 x 10 -4 (98 tests, 21 tests for three dysglycemic outcomes and seven FI clusters, and 49 tests for seven outcomes and seven FI clusters, and 28 for four liver traits by seven FI clusters).
MACAD and HTN-IR study description and genotyping.
MACAD and HTN-IR cohorts are two similar cohorts of Mexican American families recruited from the Los Angeles area, as described previously 28, 29 .
text.formatted: MACAD and HTN-IR cohorts are two similar cohorts of Mexican American families recruited from the Los Angeles area, as described previously <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">28,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">29</ref> .

text.text: We analyzed 1,316 individuals who did not have diabetes and who had undergone the euglycemic hyperinsulinemic clamp procedure, yielding direct measures of insulin sensitivity and insulin clearance.
These participants were free of major medical illness, and none were taking glucocorticoids or other drugs that could affect glucose homeostasis.
MACAD/HTN-IR participants were genotyped using the Illumina HumanOmniExpress Beadchip 30 , with subsequent imputation using 1000 Genomes phase 3.
text.formatted: MACAD/HTN-IR participants were genotyped using the Illumina HumanOmniExpress Beadchip <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">30</ref> , with subsequent imputation using 1000 Genomes phase 3.

text.text: Studies in MACAD/HTN-IR were approved by Human Subjects Protection Institutional Review Boards at UCLA, the University of Southern California, the Lundquist Institute, and Cedars-Sinai Medical Center.
All subjects gave written informed consent prior to participation.
We analyzed insulin clearance, insulin secretion, insulin sensitivity, and disposition index.
Insulin sensitivity and insulin clearance were measured in 1,316 non-diabetic individuals from the MACAD and HTN-IR cohorts via the euglycemic hyperinsulinemic clamp 30 .
text.formatted: Insulin sensitivity and insulin clearance were measured in 1,316 non-diabetic individuals from the MACAD and HTN-IR cohorts via the euglycemic hyperinsulinemic clamp <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">30</ref> .

text.text: The glucose infusion rate (M value) during the last 30 minutes of steady-state glucose and insulin levels during the clamp reflects glucose uptake by all tissues (mainly insulin-mediated glucose uptake in muscle) and is directly correlated with tissue insulin sensitivity.
The metabolic clearance rate of insulin (MCRI) was calculated as the insulin infusion rate divided by the insulin concentration during the steady state of the euglycemic clamp 31.
text.formatted: The metabolic clearance rate of insulin (MCRI) was calculated as the insulin infusion rate divided by the insulin concentration during the steady state of the euglycemic clamp <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">31</ref>.

text.text: Multipoint OGTT was available in participants from MACAD (n=512).

In those subjects, we calculated acute insulin secretion as the area under the curve (AUC) for insulin from baseline to 30 min over the corresponding AUC for glucose (AUC-Ins30/AUC-Glu30), which is highly correlated with first phase insulin secretion from the intravenous glucose tolerance test (r = 0.7) 32 .
text.formatted: In those subjects, we calculated acute insulin secretion as the area under the curve (AUC) for insulin from baseline to 30 min over the corresponding AUC for glucose (AUC-Ins30/AUC-Glu30), which is highly correlated with first phase insulin secretion from the intravenous glucose tolerance test (r = 0.7) <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">32</ref> .

text.text: This AUC-based insulin secretion measure has been found to have a hyperbolic relationship with insulin sensitivity, consistent with the relationship found when insulin secretion and insulin sensitivity are measured with gold standard physiologic tests 33 .
text.formatted: This AUC-based insulin secretion measure has been found to have a hyperbolic relationship with insulin sensitivity, consistent with the relationship found when insulin secretion and insulin sensitivity are measured with gold standard physiologic tests <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">33</ref> .

text.text: This relationship allows calculation of the disposition index, the product of insulin sensitivity and insulin secretion (M x AUC-Ins30/AUC-Glu30), which represents an index of insulin secretion that accounts for its degree of compensation for insulin resistance.

This study contributes new knowledge on FI genetic cluster associations with prediabetes, liver outcomes, and measures of insulin homeostasis using detailed physiologic phenotyping (euglycemic hyperinsulinemia clamp and OGTT) in Hispanics/Latinos, a population at high risk for type 2 diabetes and cardiometabolic complications.
We first confirmed that HCHS/SOL Hispanics/Latinos with diabetes were more likely to have type 2 diabetes versus type 1 diabetes using a type 1 diabetes PS.
We then tested FI cluster PSs and were able to reproduce patterns of association of these clusters related to distinct increased insulin mechanisms with cardiometabolic traits.
Therefore, we validated for the first time FI clustercardiometabolic trait associations in Hispanics/Latinos, providing support for the relevance of these clusters in this population.
Our findings include positive associations of the Adiposity-driven Hyperinsulinemia and inverse associations of the Lipodystrophy cluster-specific PS with obesity measures of BMI and body fat %.
The Lipodystrophy cluster-specific PS was associated with type 2 diabetes in our study.
Sevilla-González et al. described an association of the Liver/Lipid cluster with type 2 diabetes, which we could not reproduce.
Among the non-diabetogenic clusters, the Preserved IS cluster-specific PS was negatively associated with type 2 diabetes, in agreement with previously reported associations.
There were no significant associations with prediabetes, or associations with insulin use among participants with diabetes.
Our main findings were significant associations of with liver measures, which have not been previously reported.
The Adiposity-driven HI cluster-specific PS was associated with measures of liver fat, including the fatty liver index and the hepatic steatosis index.
In contrast, the Liver/Lipid cluster-specific PS was associated with measures of liver fibrosis.
Overall, these results provide insights into distinct liver outcomes for two diabetogenic hyperinsulinemia clusters related to liver fat accumulation and liver fibrosis.
Because these associations are from biomarker-derived liver indexes, further studies are needed to assess the long-term clinical liver outcomes related to these FI clusters.
Our study also found a significant association of the Liver/Lipid cluster-specific PS with low eGFR.
These results are concordant with findings from the original publication that showed associations of the Liver/Lipid cluster-specific PS with reduced lower eGFR and CKD 15.
text.formatted: These results are concordant with findings from the original publication that showed associations of the Liver/Lipid cluster-specific PS with reduced lower eGFR and CKD <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">15</ref>.

text.text: However, Sevilla-González et al. described additional associations of non-diabetogenic Preserved IS and Elevated IS clusters with CKD, which were not significant in our study.

These kidney outcome findings will need to be further investigated in large longitudinal studies to better characterize CKD patterns and disease progression related to FI clusters, and experimental studies may uncover potential mechanisms and causal relationships, if associations are confirmed.

To gain insight into the physiologic mechanisms underlying the seven FI clusters, we assessed their association with measures of insulin sensitivity, insulin secretion, insulin clearance, and disposition index.

We showed that the increased insulin secretion seen with the Elevated IS cluster could represent appropriate compensation or improved beta-cell function, a notion supported by increased disposition index.

Disposition index, a measure of the beta-cell's ability to compensate for insulin resistance, is a major determinant of diabetes risk, with higher levels of disposition index indicating lower risk of diabetes.
For other clusters, associations were not significant.
Our study is limited to FI clusters previously developed, which used SNPs from GWAS of FI from individuals of European ancestry.

Given Hispanics/Latinos have admixture of European, African and Native American ancestries, the contribution of SNPs from African and Amerindian ancestries were not included in the cluster development.

Future studies including multi-population GWAS to develop FI clusters may improve prediction of clinical outcomes, especially cardiovascular outcomes in Hispanics/Latinos, which we were not able to identify.
Additional limitations are the small number of cardiovascular events in our study, which were self-reported.

A limitation to euglycemic hyperinsulinemic clamp measures of insulin sensitivity and insulin clearance is that they measure these traits on a whole-body level, such that organspecific measures (e.g., hepatic insulin clearance vs kidney insulin clearance) are not available.
Conclusion.
This large study of Hispanics/Latinos validated cluster-specific PS clusters of FI and associations of the Lipodystrophy cluster-specific PS with type 2 diabetes.
It also identified associations of the Liver/Lipid cluster-specific PS with liver fibrosis and low eGFR, and the Adiposity-driven HI with liver fat indexes.
These findings support potential hyperinsulinemia mechanisms contributing to liver and kidney diseases.

They also demonstrate that insulin has a quantifiable heterogeneous genetic foundation related to type 2 diabetes and other outcomes in Hispanics/Latinos that may identify mechanisms for disease risk to improve patient outcomes.  clustering traits in the Hispanic Community Healthy Study / Study of Latinos.

We used a large data of the Hispanic Community Health Study/Study of Latinos (HCHS/SOL) to validate FI cluster-specific PS in Hispanics/Latinos and tested the associations of these clusters with cardiometabolic risk factors, indexes for liver fat and fibrosis, and cardiovascular and kidney outcomes.

Because FI clusters are related to type 2 diabetes mechanisms, we first use a polygenetic score to differentiate participants with type 1 diabetes from type 2 diabetes before testing the association of hyperinsulinemia cluster-specific PS with clinical outcomes.

To shed light on the pathophysiology underlying these clusters, we also assessed their association with indices of insulin homeostasis (insulin sensitivity, insulin secretion, insulin clearance, disposition index) in the Mexican American Coronary Artery Disease (MACAD) and Hypertension-Insulin Resistance (HTN-IR) cohorts that have undergone euglycemic hyperinsulinemic clamps and oral glucose tolerance tests.
